source: Rod-shaped fission yeast cells divide at a threshold size partly due to Cdr2 kinase, which forms nodes at the medial cell cortex where it inhibits the Cdk1-inhibitor Wee1.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pom1 kinase phosphorylates and inhibits Cdr2.
source: Pom1 kinase phosphorylates and inhibits Cdr2, and forms cortical concentration gradients from cell poles.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pom1 forms cortical concentration gradients from cell poles.
source: Pom1 kinase phosphorylates and inhibits Cdr2, and forms cortical concentration gradients from cell poles.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pom1 inhibits Cdr2 signaling to Wee1 specifically in small cells.
source: Pom1 inhibits Cdr2 signaling to Wee1 specifically in small cells, but the time and place of their regulatory interactions were unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is consistent with established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pom1 forms stable oligomeric clusters that dynamically sample the cell cortex.
source: We show that Pom1 forms stable oligomeric clusters that dynamically sample the cell cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data including TIRF microscopy, sucrose gradient centrifugation, and in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: Pom1 cluster binding frequency is patterned into a concentration gradient by the polarity landmarks Tea1 and Tea4.
source: Binding frequency is patterned into a concentration gradient by the polarity landmarks Tea1 and Tea4.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing altered Pom1 cluster dynamics in tea1∆ and tea4∆ mutants.

claim: Pom1 clusters colocalize with Cdr2 nodes.
source: Pom1 clusters colocalize with Cdr2 nodes, forming a glucose-modulated inhibitory threshold against node activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by two-color TIRF microscopy data showing colocalization of Pom1 clusters and Cdr2 nodes.

claim: Pom1 clusters and Cdr2 nodes form a glucose-modulated inhibitory threshold against node activation.
source: Pom1 clusters colocalize with Cdr2 nodes, forming a glucose-modulated inhibitory threshold against node activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing changes in Pom1 cluster distribution and Cdr2 node properties under different glucose conditions.

claim: Pom1-Cdr2-Wee1 operates in multiprotein clusters at the cortex to promote mitotic entry at a cell size that can be modified by nutrient availability.
source: Our work reveals how Pom1-Cdr2-Wee1 operates in multiprotein clusters at the cortex to promote mitotic entry at a cell size that can be modified by nutrient availability.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including microscopy, biochemistry, and genetic analysis.

claim: Many cell types display a remarkable ability to maintain a constant size during rapid cycles of growth and division.
source: Many cell types display a remarkable ability to maintain a constant size during rapid cycles of growth and division (Fantes and Nurse, 1977; Ginzberg et al., 2015; Jorgensen and Tyers, 2004; Fantes, 1977; Dolznig et al., 2004; Lloyd, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Cell size control is a system-level property that emerges from the integration of multiple size-dependent signal transduction pathways.
source: Such cell size control is a system-level property that emerges from the integration of multiple size-dependent signal transduction pathways.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field of cell size control.

claim: Nutritional cues and other environmental factors can alter cell size.
source: For example, nutritional cues and other environmental factors can alter cell size (Fantes and Nurse, 1977; Kelkar and Martin, 2015; Shiozaki, 2009; Yanagida et al., 2011; Young and Fantes, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Size-dependent signaling pathways lead to regulated activation of the conserved cyclin-dependent kinase Cdk1.
source: In eukaryotic cells, these signaling pathways lead to regulated activation of the conserved cyclin-dependent kinase Cdk1 (Harashima et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Activated Cdk1 triggers mitotic entry and the cascade of events that lead to cell division.
source: Activated Cdk1 triggers mitotic entry and the cascade of events that lead to cell division (Gould and Nurse, 1989; Simanis and Nurse, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: The fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe is an excellent model system to study size-dependent signaling pathways that regulate Cdk1.
source: The fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe is an excellent model system to study size-dependent signaling pathways that regulate Cdk1.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Fission yeast cells have a simple geometry that facilitates cell size studies.
source: Fission yeast cells have a simple geometry that facilitates cell size studies.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about fission yeast as a model organism.

claim: Cylindrical fission yeast cells maintain a constant cell width and grow by linear extension during interphase.
source: These cylindrical cells maintain a constant cell width, and grow by linear extension during interphase (Fantes and Nurse, 1977; Moreno et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: A network of cell polarity proteins positioned at cell tips restricts growth to these sites and maintains proper cell morphology.
source: A network of cell polarity proteins positioned at cell tips restricts growth to these sites and maintains proper cell morphology (Chang and Martin, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Cell length doubles in one cell cycle in fission yeast.
source: As a result, cell length doubles in one cell cycle, and many aspects of cell geometry scale with this increase in cell length (Gu and Oliferenko, 2019; Neumann and Nurse, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Fission yeast cells primarily measure surface area, not length or volume, for cell size control.
source: Recent studies used cell shape mutants to show that fission yeast cells primarily measure surface area, not length or volume, for cell size control (Facchetti et al., 2019; Pan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent prior work.

claim: Cdk1 activity is established by the opposing activities of the inhibitory protein kinase Wee1 and the counteracting phosphatase Cdc25.
source: Cdk1 activity is established by the opposing activities of the inhibitory protein kinase Wee1, and the counteracting phosphatase Cdc25 (Gautier et al., 1991; Gould and Nurse, 1989; Kumagai and Dunphy, 1991; Russell and Nurse, 1986; Russell and Nurse, 1987; Strausfeld et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Mutations in Wee1, Cdc25, and their upstream regulators lead to changes in cell size in fission yeast.
source: In fission yeast, mutations in Wee1, Cdc25, and their upstream regulators lead to changes in cell size.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: The cellular concentration of Cdc25 increases as cells grow during interphase.
source: The cellular concentration of Cdc25 increases as cells grow during interphase (Keifenheim et al., 2017; Moreno et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The concentration of Wee1 remains constant during interphase.
source: In contrast, the concentration of Wee1 remains constant during interphase, but it is progressively phosphorylated by the conserved inhibitory kinases Cdr1 and Cdr2 (Aligue et al., 1997; Breeding et al., 1998; Kanoh and Russell, 1998; Keifenheim et al., 2017; Lucena et al., 2017; Opalko and Moseley, 2017; Russell and Nurse, 1987; Wu and Russell, 1993; Parker et al., 1993; Coleman et al., 1993; Young and Fantes, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Wee1 is progressively phosphorylated by the conserved inhibitory kinases Cdr1 and Cdr2 during interphase.
source: In contrast, the concentration of Wee1 remains constant during interphase, but it is progressively phosphorylated by the conserved inhibitory kinases Cdr1 and Cdr2 (Aligue et al., 1997; Breeding et al., 1998; Kanoh and Russell, 1998; Keifenheim et al., 2017; Lucena et al., 2017; Opalko and Moseley, 2017; Russell and Nurse, 1987; Wu and Russell, 1993; Parker et al., 1993; Coleman et al., 1993; Young and Fantes, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: cdr2 mutants fail to divide at a constant surface area and instead divide according to cell volume or length.
source: cdr2 mutants fail to divide at a constant surface area, and instead divide according to cell volume or length (Facchetti et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cdr2-Cdr1-Wee1 signaling underlies the primary size-sensing pathway that measures cell surface area.
source: This change suggests that Cdr2-Cdr1-Wee1 signaling underlies the primary size-sensing pathway that measures cell surface area, while additional pathways related to volume and length are engaged in its absence.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited experimental results in cdr2 mutants.

claim: Cdr2 forms punctate oligomeric structures called nodes that stably bind to the medial cell cortex.
source: The localization of Cdr2, Cdr1, and Wee1 support this model (Figure 1A): Cdr2 forms punctate oligomeric structures called nodes that stably bind to the medial cell cortex, and recruits Cdr1 to these sites (Akamatsu et al., 2014; Akamatsu et al., 2017; Guzmán-Vendrell et al., 2015; Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Morrell et al., 2004; Moseley et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Cdr2 recruits Cdr1 to cortical nodes.
source: The localization of Cdr2, Cdr1, and Wee1 support this model (Figure 1A): Cdr2 forms punctate oligomeric structures called nodes that stably bind to the medial cell cortex, and recruits Cdr1 to these sites (Akamatsu et al., 2014; Akamatsu et al., 2017; Guzmán-Vendrell et al., 2015; Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Morrell et al., 2004; Moseley et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Wee1 localizes primarily in the nucleus and spindle-pole body.
source: Wee1 localizes primarily in the nucleus and spindle-pole body, where it encounters Cdk1 to prevent mitotic entry (Masuda et al., 2011; Moseley et al., 2009; Wu et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Wee1 transiently visits cortical Cdr1/2 nodes in bursts that lead to inhibition of Wee1 kinase activity.
source: In addition, Wee1 transiently visits cortical Cdr1/2 nodes in bursts that lead to inhibition of Wee1 kinase activity (Allard et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The frequency and duration of Wee1 bursts at Cdr1/2 nodes increase approximately twenty-fold as cells double in size.
source: The frequency and duration of these Wee1 bursts at Cdr1/2 nodes increase approximately twenty-fold as cells double in size (Allard et al., 2018), leading to size-dependent inhibition of Wee1 at the cell surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Increased Wee1 bursting depends upon the doubling in number of Cdr1/2 nodes during one cell cycle.
source: First, increased Wee1 bursting depends upon the doubling in number of Cdr1/2 nodes during one cell cycle, but this 2-fold increase is smaller than the 20-fold increase in Wee1 bursting (Allard et al., 2018; Deng and Moseley, 2013; Pan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The 2-fold increase in Cdr1/2 nodes is smaller than the 20-fold increase in Wee1 bursting.
source: First, increased Wee1 bursting depends upon the doubling in number of Cdr1/2 nodes during one cell cycle, but this 2-fold increase is smaller than the 20-fold increase in Wee1 bursting (Allard et al., 2018; Deng and Moseley, 2013; Pan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Activation of Cdr2 increases as cells increase in size.
source: Second, activation of Cdr2 increases as cells increase in size (Deng et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cdr2 kinase activity is required for Wee1 localization to nodes.
source: Cdr2 kinase activity is required for Wee1 localization to nodes, and is controlled by the upstream kinase Pom1 (Allard et al., 2018; Moseley et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cdr2 kinase activity is controlled by the upstream kinase Pom1.
source: Cdr2 kinase activity is required for Wee1 localization to nodes, and is controlled by the upstream kinase Pom1 (Allard et al., 2018; Moseley et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pom1 directly phosphorylates and inhibits the activation of Cdr2.
source: Pom1 directly phosphorylates and inhibits the activation of Cdr2 (Bhatia et al., 2014; Deng et al., 2014; Kettenbach et al., 2015; Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Moseley et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Pom1 phosphorylates a separate set of sites on Cdr2 to disrupt oligomerization and membrane binding.
source: Pom1 also phosphorylates a separate set of sites on Cdr2 to disrupt oligomerization and membrane binding (Bhatia et al., 2014; Rincon et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pom1 regulation of Cdr2 increases the frequency and duration of Wee1 bursts at Cdr1/2 nodes, but only in small cells.
source: Pom1 regulation of Cdr2 increases the frequency and duration of Wee1 bursts at Cdr1/2 nodes, but only in small cells (Allard et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: pom1∆ cells divide at a small size due to dysregulation of the Cdr2-Cdr1-Wee1 pathway.
source: Consistent with this defect, pom1∆ cells divide at a small size due to dysregulation of the Cdr2-Cdr1-Wee1 pathway (Bähler and Pringle, 1998; Bhatia et al., 2014; Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Moseley et al., 2009; Wood and Nurse, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Pom1 localizes in a cortical spatial gradient that is enriched at cell tips, with a lower concentration at the medial cell cortex.
source: Pom1 localizes in a cortical spatial gradient that is enriched at cell tips, with a lower concentration at the medial cell cortex, where its substrate Cdr2 forms nodes (Bähler and Pringle, 1998; Bhatia et al., 2014; Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009; Moseley et al., 2009; Bähler and Nurse, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The majority of Pom1 and Cdr2 molecules in a cell are spatially separated.
source: Thus, the majority of Pom1 and Cdr2 molecules in a cell are spatially separated (Figure 1A), raising the question of when and where they interact.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the known localization patterns of Pom1 and Cdr2, as illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Ectopic targeting of Pom1 to the medial cell cortex inhibits Cdr2 node formation and Cdr2-dependent cell size signaling.
source: For example, ectopic targeting of Pom1 to the medial cell cortex inhibits Cdr2 node formation and Cdr2-dependent cell size signaling (Martin and Berthelot-Grosjean, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The Pom1 gradient is disrupted as part of a cellular response to glucose deprivation, which leads to increased Pom1 concentration at the lateral cortex where it delays mitotic entry.
source: Additionally, the Pom1 gradient is disrupted as part of a cellular response to glucose deprivation, which leads to increased Pom1 concentration at the lateral cortex where it delays mitotic entry (Kelkar and Martin, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Pom1 functions analogously to an intracellular morphogen, acting as a concentration-dependent and localization-controlled inhibitor of Cdr2 nodes.
source: In this system, Pom1 functions analogously to an intracellular morphogen, acting as a concentration-dependent and localization-controlled inhibitor of Cdr2 nodes.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the known properties of Pom1 and its regulation of Cdr2.

claim: Levels of Pom1 at the medial cell cortex in wild-type cells growing under steady state conditions are low, constant, and do not vary with cell size.
source: However, levels of Pom1 at the medial cell cortex in wild-type cells growing under steady state conditions are low, constant, and do not vary with cell size (Bhatia et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Past studies have led to a model for Pom1 gradient formation driven by the binding and diffusion of individual Pom1 molecules in the plasma membrane.
source: Past studies have led to a model for Pom1 gradient formation driven by the binding and diffusion of individual Pom1 molecules in the plasma membrane (Hachet et al., 2011; Hersch et al., 2015; Saunders et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dynamic clusters of Pom1 have been observed and are proposed to form by unstable oligomerization of molecules diffusing on the membrane.
source: Intriguingly, dynamic clusters of Pom1 have also been observed and are proposed to form by unstable oligomerization of molecules diffusing on the membrane (Hachet et al., 2011; Saunders et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Pom1 clusters are thought to form and decay rapidly, temporarily slowing Pom1 diffusion rates and reducing noise in the gradient.
source: These clusters are thought to form and decay rapidly, temporarily slowing Pom1 diffusion rates and reducing noise in the gradient (Saunders et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Along the lateral cortex of interphase cells, Pom1-mNG was localized almost exclusively in discreet clusters, with no apparent diffuse signal.
source: Surprisingly, along the lateral cortex of interphase cells, Pom1-mNG was localized almost exclusively in discreet clusters, with no apparent diffuse signal (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In images from a single time-point, Pom1 clusters formed a noisy concentration gradient.
source: In images from a single time-point, Pom1 clusters formed a noisy concentration gradient (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: Time-averaging of Pom1 cluster images produced a smoother gradient dotted by occasional clusters.
source: Time-averaging produced a smoother gradient dotted by occasional clusters (Figure 1B,D), similar to the gradient observed by confocal microscopy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and 1D, and confocal microscopy data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Pom1 clusters were highly dynamic.
source: Pom1 clusters were highly dynamic (Video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by time-lapse TIRF microscopy shown in Video 1.

claim: Pom1 clusters appeared on the cell sides with a frequency of ~2 µm−2s−1.
source: They appeared on the cell sides with a frequency of ~2 µm−2s−1, and remained bound for less than 2 s on average (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by quantitative analysis of TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Pom1 clusters remained bound to the cell cortex for less than 2 s on average.
source: They appeared on the cell sides with a frequency of ~2 µm−2s−1, and remained bound for less than 2 s on average (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by quantitative analysis of TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: During cortical attachment, Pom1 clusters exhibited minimal diffusion which lacked directionality, and instead appeared to diffuse randomly in submicron patches of cortex.
source: During this brief cortical attachment, Pom1 clusters exhibited minimal diffusion which lacked directionality, and instead appeared to diffuse randomly in submicron patches of cortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by single-particle tracking data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,E.

claim: Mean squared displacement measurements were consistent with free diffusion of Pom1 clusters within submicron corrals.
source: Mean squared displacement (MSD) measurements were consistent with free diffusion of Pom1 clusters within submicron corrals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,C,D) (Qian et al., 1991).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B,C,D.

claim: The measured diffusion coefficient for Pom1 clusters in cells was D = 0.134 ± 0.017 µm2/s.
source: The measured diffusion coefficient (D = 0.134 ± 0.017 µm2/s) was slow for a membrane-associated protein (Knight et al., 2010; Weiß et al., 2013), likely reflecting the large size and/or multiple membrane contacts for oligomeric Pom1 clusters.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The slow diffusion coefficient of Pom1 clusters likely reflects the large size and/or multiple membrane contacts for oligomeric Pom1 clusters.
source: The measured diffusion coefficient (D = 0.134 ± 0.017 µm2/s) was slow for a membrane-associated protein (Knight et al., 2010; Weiß et al., 2013), likely reflecting the large size and/or multiple membrane contacts for oligomeric Pom1 clusters.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the measured diffusion coefficient, based on comparison to typical values for membrane-associated proteins.

claim: Pom1-mNG localized at cell tips almost entirely in clusters.
source: Similar to cell sides, Pom1-mNG localized at cell tips almost entirely in clusters (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by 'head-on' TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pom1 localization in clusters at tips was confirmed by 'head-on' confocal imaging and is not an artifact of the TIRF approach.
source: We also used 'head-on' confocal imaging to confirm that Pom1 localization in clusters at tips was not an artifact of the TIRF approach (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C); a conclusion further supported by work using high resolution wide-field microscopy (Dodgson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and a citation to prior work.

claim: Compared to cell sides, Pom1 clusters appeared twice as frequently at cell tips but with a similar cortical duration.
source: Compared to cell sides, Pom1 clusters appeared twice as frequently at cell tips but with a similar cortical duration, again exhibiting minimal and non-directional diffusion away from their binding site (Figure 1E,F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by quantitative analysis of TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1E,F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Fluorescence intensity of individual Pom1 clusters at cell tips and cell sides were similar, although a low number of brighter clusters were detected at cell tips.
source: Fluorescence intensity of individual clusters at cell tips and cell sides were similar, although we detected a low number of brighter clusters at cell tips, likely representing multiple diffraction-limited clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Airyscan super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D,E.

claim: The Pom1 gradient is formed by patterning the membrane binding frequency of cortical clusters along the long axis of the cell, rather than by diffusion of Pom1 molecules from the cell tips to the cell side.
source: From these data, we conclude that the Pom1 gradient is formed by patterning the membrane binding frequency of cortical clusters along the long axis of the cell, rather than by diffusion of Pom1 molecules from the cell tips to the cell side.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, based on the experimental data showing differential binding frequencies of Pom1 clusters at tips versus sides.

claim: High-speed continuous TIRF videos suggested that Pom1 clusters bind and release the cortex as a pre-formed unit.
source: However, our high-speed (20 ms/frame) continuous TIRF videos suggested that Pom1 clusters bind and release the cortex as a pre-formed unit (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by high-speed TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In rare cell lysis events during TIRF imaging, Pom1 clusters remained intact in extruded cytoplasm.
source: Consistent with this possibility, in the rare cases when we observed cell lysis events during TIRF imaging, Pom1 clusters remained intact in extruded cytoplasm (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Clusters of Pom1-mNG were observed in extracts made from Pom1-mNG cells, but not from untagged wild-type cells.
source: Using TIRF microscopy, we observed clusters of Pom1-mNG in extracts made from Pom1-mNG cells, but not from untagged wild-type cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by TIRF microscopy of cell extracts shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Most Pom1 exists in a large 60S complex in detergent cell extracts.
source: By fractionating detergent cell extracts from pom1-3xHA cells, we found that most Pom1 exists in a large 60S complex, consistent with Pom1 clusters observed in cells and with previous results from gel filtration (Bähler and Nurse, 2001).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by velocity sucrose gradient sedimentation data shown in Figure 2C, and is consistent with prior work.

claim: Fractions 6–8 containing the 60S Pom1 peak, when dialyzed and centrifuged on a second sucrose gradient, again sedimented at 60S, indicating that they represent a stable complex.
source: Fractions 6–8 containing this peak were dialyzed and centrifuged on a second sucrose gradient. These pooled fractions again sedimented at 60S, indicating that they represent a stable complex (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by velocity sucrose gradient sedimentation data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B,C.

claim: Pom1-mNG clusters from cytoplasmic extracts bind and release supported lipid bilayers with strikingly similar dynamics as in cells.
source: In this cell free-system, Pom1-mNG clusters bound and released SLB lipids with strikingly similar dynamics as in cells (Figure 2E,F, Video 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by TIRF microscopy of Pom1 clusters on supported lipid bilayers shown in Figure 2E,F and Video 2.

claim: MSD measurements for Pom1 clusters on SLBs revealed a diffusion coefficient similar to that measured in cells (Dcell = 0.134 ± 0.017 µm2/s vs DSLB = 0.168 ± 0.018 µm2/s).
source: MSD measurements for Pom1 clusters on SLBs revealed a diffusion coefficient similar to that measured in cells (Dcell = 0.134 ± 0.017 µm2/s vs DSLB = 0.168 ± 0.018 µm2/s), but the relationship was linear over the lifetime of most particles (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B,C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B,C,D.

claim: Whereas membrane diffusion of Pom1 clusters in cells is confined within microdomains, clusters can diffuse without confinement on synthetic bilayers.
source: These results indicate that whereas membrane diffusion of Pom1 clusters in cells is confined within microdomains, clusters can diffuse without confinement on synthetic bilayers.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of MSD measurements in cells versus on supported lipid bilayers.

claim: Dwell times of Pom1 clusters on supported lipid bilayers were increased for the kinase-dead mutant Pom1(K728R)-mNG.
source: Dwell times were increased for the kinase-dead mutant Pom1(K728R)-mNG, which was previously shown to increase cortical Pom1 levels in cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) (Bähler and Pringle, 1998; Hachet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and citations to prior work.

claim: Pom1 clusters did not colocalize with Cdr2 nodes in detergent extracts.
source: Pom1 clusters did not colocalize with Cdr2 nodes in detergent extracts, suggesting they remain as separate structures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by TIRF microscopy of cell extracts shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The majority of cellular Pom1 protein is contained within discreet, highly-stable oligomers that bind and release membranes with kinetics dictated by their catalytic activity in a pattern that generates a concentration gradient.
source: Collectively, our TIRF microscopy and in vitro analysis of Pom1 clusters support a model whereby the majority of cellular Pom1 protein is contained within discreet, highly-stable oligomers that bind and release membranes with kinetics dictated by their catalytic activity in a pattern that generates a concentration gradient.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, based on multiple lines of experimental evidence including TIRF microscopy, sucrose gradient centrifugation, and in vitro reconstitution experiments.

claim: Recombinant GST-Pom1 sedimented in a low molecular weight peak unlike Pom1 clusters from cells.
source: Recombinant GST-Pom1 sedimented in a low molecular weight peak unlike Pom1 clusters from cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Purified GST-Pom1 was assembled into a cluster-sized high molecular weight complex by incubation with wild-type yeast detergent extract.
source: Remarkably, purified GST-Pom1 was assembled into a cluster-sized high molecular weight complex by incubation with wild-type yeast detergent extract (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Complex formation of GST-Pom1 was also induced by incubation with pom1∆ cell extracts, meaning that additional cellular factors drive this assembly process.
source: Complex formation was also induced by incubation of GST-Pom1 with pom1∆ cell extracts, meaning that additional cellular factors drive this assembly process (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by sucrose gradient sedimentation data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Once assembled, Pom1 clusters are stable oligomeric complexes with intrinsic membrane-binding properties that can be reconstituted in vitro.
source: Once assembled, Pom1 clusters are stable oligomeric complexes with intrinsic membrane-binding properties that can be reconstituted in vitro.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing that Pom1 clusters can be assembled in vitro and exhibit membrane-binding properties.

claim: Additional cellular regulatory proteins are likely to promote the binding of Pom1 clusters at cell tips, leading to the spatial gradient.
source: Additional cellular regulatory proteins are likely to promote the binding of Pom1 clusters at cell tips, leading to the spatial gradient.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that Pom1 clusters bind more frequently at cell tips than at cell sides.

claim: Tea4 is required for localization of Pom1 to the cortex.
source: However, past studies have shown that Tea1 and Tea4 have distinct mechanistic roles: Tea4 is required for localization of Pom1 to the cortex, whereas Tea1 is required for enrichment of cortical Pom1 to the cell tip (Hachet et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Tea1 is required for enrichment of cortical Pom1 to the cell tip.
source: However, past studies have shown that Tea1 and Tea4 have distinct mechanistic roles: Tea4 is required for localization of Pom1 to the cortex, whereas Tea1 is required for enrichment of cortical Pom1 to the cell tip (Hachet et al., 2011).
